t: Minimum Amount of Time to Fill Cups — Max vs Half-Sum Bound
o: Each second serves at most 2 cups, so we need at least ceil(total/2) seconds. Also, cups of the most numerous type can only be filled one per second when the other types run dry, giving a lower bound of max(amount). Both bounds are simultaneously achievable by always pairing the two largest types, so the answer is max(max(amount), ceil(sum/2)). Check: [1,4,2] gives max(4, ceil(7/2)=4) = 4; [5,4,4] gives max(5, ceil(13/2)=7) = 7; [5,0,0] gives max(5, 3) = 5.
k: Answer = max(largest pile, ceiling of total/2); pairing the two biggest piles each second attains it.

a.i: Compute the sum and maximum; return the larger of the two lower bounds. Correctness follows from an exchange argument: while at least two types remain, serve the two largest, which keeps both bounds tight.
s: total = amount[0]+amount[1]+amount[2]; mx = max of the three.
a.t: O(1) — constant work over three values.

a.i: Repeatedly pop the two largest counts, decrement both, and push back, counting seconds. This directly implements the optimal strategy and doubles as a proof-by-construction; with values <= 100 it terminates quickly.
s: Push nonzero amounts into a max-heap.
Each second: pop up to two largest, decrement, re-push positives, increment answer.
a.t: O(S log 3) where S is the total cup count (at most 300 steps).

w: Quote the formula in an interview and justify with the two lower bounds; the heap simulation is a nice sanity check. Pitfall: integer division rounding — use ceiling of total/2. Generalizes to k drink types with the same max-vs-half-sum style bound only for k=3.
